newsitem.title: UK: UK equities weigh up life under Labour. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UK equities weigh up life under Labour. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]

text.p: It has been a long time since the British stock market has had to live with a Labour Party government and its memories of the dying days of the last one are coloured by thoughts of high inflation and strikes.

Now, after 18 years of Conservative Party rule, opinion polls say Labour's Tony Blair is odds-on to lead his party to victory in Thursday's election. Investors have already spent months trying to analyse the implications.
However, despite the market's knee-jerk antipathy towards a Labour administration, there are historical precedents for the stock market to perform well under Labour.

Between Harold Wilson's Labour victory of October 1974 for instance and the election of the Conservatives under Margaret Thatcher in May 1979, the FT-All Share index quadrupled in value from just above 60 to over 280.

And after a previous Wilson government's devaluation of early 1967, the index leapt from around 95 to end the year at around 120. By contrast the bear market of 1973 and 1974 mostly occurred under the Conservative government of Edward Heath.
Such raw figures however can be misleading, since they take no account of inflation or of the market's relative performance compared with other leading markets.

Anyway the world, and the Labour party, has changed a lot since the late seventies. Blair and Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown have worked hard to present a business-friendly front designed in part to keep the markets on their side.

One measure of the market's relaxed stance on the prospect of a Labour regime came in the Wall Street-led rally in the final week of the campaign, with the FTSE 100 index rising sharply in the last two days to trade around its record high on Wednesday before easing back.
Previous Labour victories, such as in 1966 and 1974, were preceded by stock market declines in the week before the result.
Whether Labour proves true to its economic promises however remains to be seen, and much policy detail remains to be spelt out.
"We know Brown is going to be tough at the macro economic level but what we don't know what the detailed policies will be," said Mark Tinker, strategist at investment bank UBS.
Worries over Labour policies have overshadowed the market for some months -- one reason the FTSE 100 has underperformed other leading indexes this year.
For the equity market the central issue is likely to be Labour's overall handling of the economy and it is here that a key test is likely to come in the weeks after the election.
With economic growth poised to increase through 1997 while government debt remains high, the incoming government faces tough decisions on how much to raise taxes and interest rates.

There are specific areas of tax policy too that could have a significant bearing on shares. Most obviously Labour is comitted to a multi-billion pound "windfall" tax on privatised utilities, designed to finance training and employment measures.

The party is expected to take a tougher line on takeovers, breaking the free market philosophy of recent years that has helped return billions of pounds for investment funds to reinvest in the market.

Other possibilities are that Labour will introduce shareholding rules to discourage over-active trading by investment funds in favour of long-term investment, and that it will reduce tax concessions that boost the value of company dividends to pension funds.

Yet even as the FTSE 100 touched a record 4,466.5 on the eve of the poll, stock market strategists said Wall Street's influence was continuing to call the shots in the UK regardless of domestic factors.
The market's first post-election hurdle will come as early as Friday with the U.S. employment report for April -- which will be regarded as a key indicator of interest rate trends in the near term.
Meantime strategists said UK shares could stage a "relief" rally on Friday as the electoral uncertainty was at last dispelled, assuming that the outcome is not a "hung" parliament.

"We have had a long campaign which has left the markets exhausted, and if we get a sizeable Labour majority the market will probably go up," said Corey Miller, of Credit Lyonnais Laing (corrects to insert full name and company).

"But we may well find it difficult to secure those gains as the market starts to think what Labour really means," Miller said. "There's a general feeling that Labour will prove less business friendly than the Conservatives have been."
